title: Risotto Milanese
subtitle: Saffron risotto from Milan
excerpt: Risotto alla Milanese is a golden, deeply savoury rice dish from Lombardy, coloured and flavoured by saffron and finished with a generous amount of butter and parmesan. It is traditionally served alongside osso buco but stands alone as a first course. The technique is straightforward once you understand the rhythm of adding stock one ladle at a time.
sourceNotes: Risotto alla Milanese originates in the Lombardy region of northern Italy and is traditionally served alongside osso buco. Saffron gives it both its golden colour and distinctive floral flavour.

content.text: Good risotto is about attention, not complexity. The rice needs stock added gradually and constant gentle stirring so that the starch releases slowly into the liquid, building the creamy consistency that defines the dish. Bloom the saffron in a small amount of warm stock before adding it: this extracts more colour and flavour than dropping it in dry. White wine is traditional: add a small glass (about 100ml) after the onion softens and let it cook off completely before adding the first ladle of stock. If you prefer to cook without alcohol, skip it and start with stock straight away.

items.prepNote: kept hot in a separate pan

content.text: Pour the stock into a saucepan and bring it to a gentle simmer. Keep it hot on the hob throughout cooking: cold stock added to the risotto will drop the temperature and disrupt the cooking process. Bloom the saffron in 2 tablespoons of the warm stock and set aside.

Melt half the butter in a wide, heavy-based pan over a medium-low heat. Add the diced onion with a pinch of salt and cook gently for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until completely soft but not coloured.
Add the rice to the pan and stir for 2 minutes until the grains are coated in butter and look slightly translucent at the edges. This toasting step is important: it gives the risotto structure.

Add the bloomed saffron and its liquid and stir to combine. Begin adding the hot stock one ladle at a time (roughly 80 to 100 ml per addition). Stir continuously after each addition and wait until the liquid is almost fully absorbed before adding the next ladle.

Continue adding stock and stirring for 18 to 20 minutes in total. The risotto is ready when the rice is tender with a very slight bite at the centre and the mixture flows slowly when you tilt the pan: this is the consistency Italians call all'onda, meaning in waves.

Remove the pan from the heat. Add the remaining butter and the grated parmesan in one go. Beat vigorously with a wooden spoon for 1 to 2 minutes until the butter melts and emulsifies into the rice, giving the risotto a glossy, creamy finish. This step is called mantecatura and is what separates a good risotto from a great one.
Taste and adjust seasoning with salt. Serve immediately in warmed bowls: risotto waits for no one. A little extra parmesan at the table is welcome.

items.symptom: The risotto is gluey and stodgy rather than creamy
items.cause: Too much stirring at too high a heat, or the stock was added too fast, causing the starch to over-release and the rice to become pasty.
items.fix: Steady, consistent stirring at medium-low heat is the target. The rice should always be moving but the heat should never be so high that the liquid boils furiously.

items.symptom: The rice is still chalky in the centre after the cooking time
items.cause: The stock was added in too large quantities at once, or the heat was too low, slowing the cooking of the starch inside each grain.
items.fix: Add another ladle of hot stock and keep stirring until the grain is just tender with the faintest bite remaining.

items.symptom: The risotto has seized up and is stiff by the time it reaches the table
items.cause: Risotto continues to absorb liquid after it leaves the heat. If it sits in the pan or in bowls, the residual starch firms it up quickly.
items.fix: Serve the moment the mantecatura is done. If it has thickened in the pan before you serve, stir in a small ladle of hot stock to loosen it back to a flowing consistency.
